sentences.text: Elaphrosaurus was a medium-sized, lightly built dinosaur that reached a length of 6.2 meters, stood 1.46 meters high at the hip, and weighed about 210 kilograms.
Its leg bones show that the shin bone was 608 millimeters long, significantly longer than the thigh bone which measured 520 millimeters, while the foot bones were 74 percent the length of the thigh.
Knowledge of this animal comes mainly from a single nearly complete skeleton, which includes the backbone, pelvis, and hind limb, but no skull has ever been found.
The name given to the genus means "light-legged lizard," a reference to its supposed running speed derived from Greek words.
One researcher noted that this creature was the longest-bodied and shallowest-chested theropod he had ever examined.
Dinosaur footprints from Niger and Jerusalem have been attributed to this species, though this assignment is considered inconclusive.
The type specimen was recovered from the Middle Dinosaur Member of the Tendaguru Formation in the Lindi Region of Tanzania.
Werner Janensch described and named the genus and its type species in 1920.
The limb proportions likely indicate it was adapted for running, a trait shared with some ornithomimosaurians.
The neck vertebrae were less flexible than those of other theropods, suggesting it supported a relatively small skull.
Anatomical traits suggest it was not a predator of large prey and may have been omnivorous or herbivorous, a view supported by its close relationship with Limusaurus.
Paul suggested that the animal likely hunted small and swift ornithopod herbivores rather than the larger sauropods and stegosaurs in its environment.
Recent studies classify Elaphrosaurus within the Ceratosauria, and a 2016 study concluded it was an early member of the Noasauridae forming a distinct group called Elaphrosaurinae.
Janensch originally described it as a coelurosaurian, but the genus now includes only one species, E. bambergi.

Elaphrosaurus bambergi lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 154 to 147 million years ago, in the Titonian stage, and also during the Kimmeridgian stage approximately 157 to 152 million years ago.
Studies suggest the paleoenvironment of the Tendaguru Formation was a marginal marine environment containing both non-marine fauna and flora.

It is debated whether Elaphrosaurus was a carnivore, omnivore, or herbivore, with some researchers suggesting it was omnivorous or herbivorous due to its relation with Limusaurus, while the time range for the genus extends from the Kimmeridgian to the Cenomanian, spanning from 154.8 to 93.9 million years ago.
